title: Armstrong's split upper lip and heavy pressure
summary: Briggs saw pus coming from Armstrong's upper lip and attributes it to heavy pressure from overwork and lack of training, saying his playing never recovered its early precision.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: And Louie stayed with her, about six -- about three months, 'cause Louie, at the time he was having a little lip trouble, too, 'cause they worked him to death.
Okay, so tell me about that. Tell me about that. What kind of trouble was he having?
He was having -- his chops were -- I don't know what happened, but there was pus coming out of his upper lip.
Pus coming out of the upper lip?
Yes. I saw that
Briggs 256
myself.
Well, what would make that happen.
You see, Louie did not have the tuition that we had.
Right.
That's that strong mouth playing. Pressing the mouthpiece to the lips.
He was using a lot of pressure?
Pressure, pressure.
Now another thing that I think I've seen about Louie is that he played on the soft part of his lip.
Yeh.
Like this.
Yeh.
Is that right?
Yes. Half and half.
Would he be up in
Briggs
here a little bit? Yes, half and half.
So he would be getting a lot of pressure right in --
Yeh.
In other words, instead of pulling down like this, he just flattened it out?
Yes.
Is that right?
Yes, that's right. That's right; yes, sir, that's right.
So that's what was causing a lot of the trouble?
That was causing a whole lot of trouble, and with that pressure, pressure, that strong arm -- what we call a strong arm,
Strong arm.
That played -- gave him a -- he has never been any -- I mean, he
Briggs
No.
Between you and I.
Well, you think his lip was never all right after that?

Never. 'Cause Louie, if you listen to "Cornet Chop Suey," that was almost like a -- what you would call a -- "Cornet Chop Suey," was almost like a recital, a trumpet recital. And if you listen to Louie after his, after his appearance in England, that's when he -- I mean his name and reputation was there -- that's going, but we can cut -- 'cause I'm not saying -- I'm just saying where.
Right, sure.
He was not the same Louie as in "Cornet Chop Suey," and the other numbers, you see. It all came from that strong mountain playing lips. That is they worked him
Briggs 259
to death. They worked him so hard that he had no other alternative, but to press in order to get the results that he wanted.
He thought he -- by using pressure that he would get the results that he wanted. By using pressure though, he just smothered his lips, you see.
And it was on the upper lip, mainly?
Yes.
Then he must have split it, did he have an infection in there?
Yes, I'm sure that he did, I tell you, there was puss coming out.
